extracted.intended_audience: federal agency rulemaking officials, eRulemaking program staff, agency counsel, and regulatory docket managers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for federal agencies on identifying, processing, and responding to mass comment campaigns, malattributed (fraudulent) comments, and computer-generated comments in notice-and-comment rulemaking. Includes recommended technologies, docket-management practices, coordination, training, and transparency measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Mass comment response
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'mass comment response' occurs when an agency receives an unusually large number of comments (e.g., hundreds or thousands) compared to what it typically receives for that rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No fixed numeric threshold is defined; as a general matter a mass comment response will feature at least an order of magnitude increase (e.g., 10x) in the number of comments received vis-à-vis a typical rulemaking for that agency. Thresholds will vary by agency and rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Mass comment campaign
rubrics_metrics.description: A special case of a mass comment response in which one or more organizations have successfully urged a large number of individuals or groups to submit comments or have submitted comments in others' names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize campaigns that produce identical or nearly identical submissions; such campaigns have grown with lower participation costs enabled by email and the internet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Malattributed comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments falsely attributed to persons by whom they were not, in fact, submitted (sometimes referred to as 'fraudulent' comments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Malattribution can take the form of using real people's names without their knowledge or inventing identities. Easy access to large datasets and automation tools has made malattribution easier; agencies should focus on attribution issues (distinct from false substantive statements in comment bodies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Computer-generated comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments that are generated by a software algorithm, replacing both human content generation and human interaction with the agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although a human creates the software, once automated it can repeatedly produce and submit comments. While earlier examples were crude, advances in NLP (e.g., GPT-style models) can produce human-quality text that is difficult to distinguish from human-written comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal responsiveness requirement: respond to 'significant' comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the APA agencies must 'consider' relevant matter presented and respond in the final rule to 'significant' comments—those that, 'if true, . . . would require a change in [the] proposed rule.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to respond to significant comments can be grounds for remand under the arbitrary-and-capricious standard. However, agencies need not respond to comments that are purely speculative or that do not disclose a factual or policy basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use de-duplication software to identify unique content
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ software to detect and identify duplicate or near-identical comments and isolate the unique informational content in the docket.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is already commonplace and recommended to reduce processing burdens associated with large numbers of duplicates. De-duplication helps agencies focus on unique substantive input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish policies regarding posting duplicate and near-identical comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt and publish a clear policy on how duplicate and near-identical comments will be handled and displayed in the docket.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options include posting a single representative example with a count of duplicates and an option to view all comments; breaking out non-identical content; and providing enhanced search options based on unique information content. Policies should balance user-friendliness, transparency, and informational completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require clarity/transparency when excluding or removing comments
rubrics_metrics.description: If an agency decides to exclude or remove duplicates, malattributed, or computer-generated comments from the docket, it should articulate such a policy in advance or provide a reasoned explanation after excluding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presumption is that agencies must place all comments in the docket; exclusion requires affirmative justification articulated in law or agency policy (examples: profanity, threats, copyrighted material).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt submission-stage tools: bulk submission, identity validation, reCAPTCHA
rubrics_metrics.description: At the comment-submission stage, agencies should consider tools that manage bulk submission and authenticate identity and human presence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations.gov provides an API facilitating bulk submissions, identity-validation features for authorized bulk users, and reCAPTCHA to screen non-humans. Agencies that do not use regulations.gov should consider similar tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stay abreast of developments in submission and detection technologies
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies and coordinating bodies should monitor technological developments related to mass, malattributed, and computer-generated comments and update countermeasures as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain situational awareness because both offending techniques and detection/mitigation technologies evolve rapidly; coordination with private-sector experts and vendors is advised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate and share best practices; provide training
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies and coordinating bodies should share best practices and innovations and provide ongoing staff training to respond to evolving technologies and supplemental participation processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training and staff development should be ongoing. Agencies should work with eRulemaking and other coordinating bodies to improve existing technologies and develop new tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: eRulemaking Program should provide a common de-duplication platform
rubrics_metrics.description: The eRulemaking Program should supply a shared de-duplication platform for agencies to use, while allowing agencies to modify or use alternative platforms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A common platform can reduce duplicated effort; coordinating bodies should also work with agencies and private vendors to develop technologies addressing common issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt posting of comments to the docket
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should post comments promptly upon receipt to the rulemaking docket when those comments are to be included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompt posting enables external correction (e.g., individuals noticing malattribution) and facilitates public evaluation and control of problematic submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy for malattributed comments: anonymize or remove
rubrics_metrics.description: If an agency is aware that a comment is malattributed, it should either retain the comment but remove the malattribution (render it anonymous) or remove the comment from the docket altogether.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anonymization protects individuals whose identities were used. Agencies are not required to affirmatively search the docket for malattributed comments, but may set reasonable policies permitting rejection or remediation of comments that violate policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not discard computer-generated comments; segregate/treat separately
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should not discard computer-generated comments even if they are segregated and treated separately from human comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Computer-generated comments may be retained but flagged or segregated; if an agency relies on such a comment it must be placed and retained in the docket.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain in docket any comment (duplicative, malattributed, or computer-generated) that agency relies upon
rubrics_metrics.description: If an agency actually relies on a duplicative, malattributed, or computer-generated comment in its rulemaking, that comment must be placed and retained in the docket.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may anonymize malattributed comments or flag/segregate computer-generated comments retained in the docket, but reliance requires retention for transparency and judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide opportunities for individuals to request removal of comments attached to their names
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow (to the extent practicable) individuals whose names have been attached to comments they did not submit to identify and request removal of such comments from the docket, potentially even after the comment deadline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This remedial channel supports correcting malattributions; agencies should consider practical mechanisms and timelines for such requests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notify submitters if agency flags or removes their comment and contact info exists
rubrics_metrics.description: If an agency flags a comment as malattributed or computer-generated or removes such a comment from the docket and the submitter provided electronic contact information, the agency should notify the submitter of the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notification increases transparency and allows affected parties to respond or seek correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide materials explaining what information is useful to commenters
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies and coordinating bodies should provide explanatory materials (e.g., videos, FAQs) telling prospective commenters what information is useful to the agency in a public comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different formats can reach different audiences and improve the quality of submissions by clarifying expectations and useful content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask specific questions and identify useful information in NPRMs/NOIs/ANPRs
rubrics_metrics.description: In notices of proposed rulemaking, notices of inquiry, and advance notices of proposed rulemaking, agencies should ask specific questions and identify particular information that would be useful in developing the proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Targeted questions make it easier for the public to provide meaningful, relevant input and improve the signal-to-noise ratio in comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: When publishing final rule, disclose removal of malattributed/computer-generated comments
rubrics_metrics.description: When publishing a final rule, agencies should state whether they removed from the docket any malattributed and/or computer-generated comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public disclosure of such removals enhances transparency and public trust in the rulemaking process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider affirmative identification efforts for malattributed/computer-generated comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should consider taking affirmative steps to identify comments that are malattributed or computer-generated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such steps may include deploying detection technologies, collaborating with coordinating bodies, and using vendor expertise. Agencies are free to set reasonable policies on detection and remediation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance user-friendliness, transparency, and informational completeness in docket presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: When designing policies and technical presentation of docketed comments, agencies should balance competing values such as ease-of-use for the public, transparency of the record, and retaining informational completeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design choices (e.g., representative posting with counts vs. full posting) should consider these values and be articulated in published policies.
